data.description:
Eye Exam Coverage Outside Medicare (2026): What to Know About VSP's Routine Vision Benefits by Better Business Advice

Eye Exam Coverage Outside Medicare (2026): What to Know About VSP's Routine Vision Benefits by Better Business Advice

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Nov. 27, 2026

NEW YORK, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- VSP ® Vision Care offers standalone vision coverage that can help eligible members manage routine eye exam and eyewear expenses not generally covered by Original Medicare*. Through its VSP Individual Vision Plans, including Standard, EasyOptions, Enhanced, and EyewearOnly, VSP provides different benefit structures for consumers considering individual vision insurance.

Eye Exam Coverage Outside Medicare

  • VSP Individual Vision Plans – individual vision insurance from VSP Vision Care covers routine eye exams, glasses, and lens enhancements separate from Medicare and employer-sponsored benefits.

Better Business Advice examines how VSP Individual Vision Plans routine vision benefits work, what consumers should know about vision coverage that is separate from Medicare, and which plan details may matter when evaluating options during the annual Medicare Open Enrollment period.

What Medicare Covers for Routine Eye Care

Original Medicare consists of Part A and Part B. Although it covers certain medically necessary eye services, routine eye exams for prescribing or fitting glasses or contact lenses are generally not covered.

Some eye-related services may qualify under specific Medicare coverage rules. These include certain glaucoma screenings for eligible individuals and specific tests or treatments for eye diseases. Prescription lenses may also be covered in limited circumstances following covered cataract surgery.

Routine vision care is a different category. An appointment to examine overall eye health and update a prescription for glasses or contact lenses is generally considered a routine exam and is generally not covered by Medicare, although Medicare may cover medically necessary services.

Understanding Standalone Vision Insurance

For people who need routine eye exams or prescription glasses, standalone vision insurance is one option to consider. This type of policy is purchased separately from Medicare and has its own premiums, covered services, copays, limitations, and provider network.

Depending on the policy, benefits may include routine eye exams, prescription lenses, frames, contact lenses, and certain lens enhancements. Coverage does not necessarily pay for every service or purchase in full. The amount a member pays depends on the selected plan and its terms.

VSP offers standalone vision coverage through VSP Individual Vision Plans. The plans are designed to help members manage eligible routine vision costs. They are separate from Medicare and are not Medicare Supplement insurance, so consumers should evaluate them on their own, apart from any medical coverage they already have.

VSP Individual Vision Plan Options and Routine Vision Benefits

VSP Individual Vision Plans currently offers four plan options: Standard, EasyOptions, Enhanced, and EyewearOnly. Each has a different benefit structure, so comparing the current plan documents is important before making an enrollment decision.

Standard, EasyOptions, and Enhanced each include coverage for a routine exam and eyewear benefits. Consumers may want to compare exam copays, frame and lens coverage, contact lens benefits, and any allowances or frequency limits.

EyewearOnly may be a fit for people who mainly want coverage for glasses or contacts and have a valid vision prescription.

Plan availability and benefit details vary by state. Premiums, copayments, allowances, exclusions, and other conditions should be confirmed using the current state-specific materials. A general plan description may not reflect the exact terms available in every location.

Comparing Vision Coverage During Medicare Open Enrollment

Medicare Open Enrollment, October 15 through December 7 this year, is an opportunity to review Medicare health and prescription drug coverage for the following year. Standalone vision insurance is not part of Medicare Open Enrollment, but this time of year can be a good reminder to review expected health care costs.

People with Medicare Advantage should first check whether their current plan already includes routine eye exams, eyewear allowances, or other vision benefits, since a separate vision policy may overlap with that coverage. VSP also states that its individual vision plans do not coordinate benefits with Medicare or any other plan. Allowances from other plans cannot be combined with a VSP Individual Vision Plan.

People with Original Medicare may have different considerations. Since routine eye exams for prescription eyewear are generally not covered, a separate vision policy may be worth comparing with the expected cost of paying out of pocket.

A practical comparison should include:

  • Annual premiums: Calculate the total cost of maintaining the policy for a full year.
  • Exam benefits: Check the exam copay, how often exams are covered, and any provider requirements.
  • Eyewear benefits: Review frame allowances, lens coverage, contact lens benefits, and the cost of lens enhancements.
  • Network access: Confirm that preferred eye doctors are in network.
  • Limitations: Read exclusions, waiting periods, benefit restrictions, and state-specific terms.

The goal is to compare the full cost of coverage with likely expenses, rather than relying on a single allowance or advertised savings estimate.

Making an Informed Coverage Decision

VSP Individual Vision Plans provide an option for people researching vision coverage outside Medicare. VSP Individual Vision Plans include several plan structures, allowing consumers to compare routine exam and eyewear benefits against their expected needs.

Before enrolling, consumers should review current premiums, covered services, copays, allowances, exclusions, and provider requirements. State-specific plan documents confirm the exact benefits available. Questions about specific retailers, eyewear products, or services should be addressed with VSP or the participating provider before making a purchase.

Better Business Advice's coverage of the topic highlights the importance of understanding the distinction between Medicare medical benefits and separate routine vision coverage. Medicare Open Enrollment offers a timely opportunity to review healthcare expenses, while a careful comparison of standalone policies can help consumers assess whether additional vision coverage fits their budget and needs.

For the full review, visit Better Business Advice.

*Check your Medicare plan to see if your vision care needs are covered and/or if a VSP Individual Vision Plan is right for you. VSP Individual Vision Plans do not coordinate benefits with Medicare or any other plan.

data.title: SAP reportedly to cut 10,000 jobs. It marks the latest in a brutal year for tech layoffs.
data.description:
By Nora Redmond

SAP is reportedly discussing cutting at least 10,000 jobs.

SAP is reportedly considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs in a heavy year of layoffs for the technology industry, withe more workforce reductions in the U.S. than any other sector.

The German software company (SAP) (XE:SAP) is discussing a restructuring set to affect about 9% to 10% of its overall workforce as it seeks to transition the business amid the artificial-intelligence boom, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to Bloomberg. The total number of job cuts has not yet been finalized and could change following negotiations with employee representative groups.

"The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful. As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures," an SAP spokesperson told MarketWatch.

The company is Germany's biggest by market capitalization, with a value of around EUR226.67 billion ($248.49 billion). It marks the latest of the European country's major blue-chip companies to contemplate significant headcount reductions, with carmaker Volkswagen (XE:VOW) planning to slash 100,000 jobs and engineering firm Thyssenkrupp (XE:TKA) shedding 4,000 roles.

And the trend extends beyond Germany, with the tech industry as a whole experiencing a wave of layoffs from the beginning of the year right through to the end as more capital is allocated to the development of AI - and as the tool becomes more capable of performing complex human tasks.

The sector accounts for 28% of total job cuts in the U.S. in 2026, making it responsible for more layoffs than any other industry, according to October's Challenger, Gray and Christmas layoff report. Tech companies announced that they were axing 5,576 roles last month, the lowest in the year so far, yet still an increase of 21% year-on-year.

Through October, tech has been responsible for 171,501 layoffs, already exceeding 154,445 cuts the sector accounted for in the entirety of 2025. And, as the report only includes employees who accept an offer in cases of voluntary redundancy programs, Microsoft's voluntary exit offer to 60,000 workers has not even been included in the figures.

"These offers tend to signal more layoffs to come. Voluntary exit offers are a softer way to shrink. They let a company reduce headcount while giving employees a choice and a cushion," wrote Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer.

-Nora Redmond

data.title: Moody's Upgrades Vietnam's Sovereign Rating to Ba1
data.description:
By Jihye Lee

Moody's Ratings upgraded Vietnam's sovereign credit rating by one notch to Ba1 from Ba2, citing improving governance and the economy's shift toward higher-value-added industries.

The ratings company on Friday also changed its outlook to stable from positive. Institutional overhauls, robust growth prospects and a more diversified economy have strengthened Vietnam's ability to withstand shocks, Moody's said.

"Reforms have streamlined public administration and judicial processes, strengthened accountability and anticorruption controls and improved the regulatory environment," Moody's said, pointing to governance as a key driver of the ratings upgrade.

However, rapid credit growth and high leverage continue to pose risks to financial stability, it added. Vulnerabilities in Vietnam's banking sector and institutional risks may weaken Vietnam's credit profile, Moody's said.

data.title: This investment strategist is 100% in cash - and warns that buying the Nasdaq dip is like catching a falling knife
data.description:
By Jules Rimmer

42 Macro strategist thinks the Fed is three moves away from neutral

A career spent catching knives will be a brief one, says 42 Macro's Darius Dale

Just because Nasdaq briefly entered bear-market territory this week, that's no reason in itself to buy stock, is the message from the head of one investment research service.

Darius Dale, founder and chief executive of the investment research boutique 42 Macro has advice for investors who think it is: "Research shows that if you try to make a career out of catching falling knives, you're not going to have a career for very long.'

For Dale, far better to "be the second investor in a confirmed trade, not the first in an unconfirmed."

Dale was articulating his extremely cautious opinions on the David Lin Report podcast, aired Thursday,. Opinions that are so cautious, his KISS model portfolio (standing for "Keep it Simple and Systematic") shifted into 80% cash at the end of September and has for the last few weeks actually been 100% cash.

Justifying this bearish stance he replied to Lin's suggestion that one might just buy stocks because they've declined so much, "that's just not what we do. We have a risk management system that's looking for signals to confirm" a move like that.

The main reason for Dale's extreme caution is that the Federal Reserve, for credibility's sake, needs to hike in December, and probably again in March to shore up its inflation-fighting credentials. "If they don't hike in December, they might as well close the institution," he says. Right now, Dale's models calculate the Fed is three 25-basis point hikes away from a policy that could be described as neutral.

The Fed is expected to tighten into the first half of 2027

It's not just inflation forcing rates higher. Dale's Wall Street contacts indicate to him that the hyperscalers (AMZN) (GOOG) (MSFT) may issue as much as $1 trillion in debt over the next few years, triple what they raised this year. That adds upward pressure on the cost of capital.

Dale cites many factors suggesting the economy is running too hot, highlighting supercore personal consumption expenditure at 4.2% year-over-year. It may take then, in Dale's opinion, until the second half of 2027 for the narrative to shift from a restrictive to a more accommodative approach, creating a policy tailwind to support equities, metals and bitcoin (BTCUSD).

As well as its KISS model, 42 Macro also runs a "Dr Mo" portfolio, representing a discretionary risk management overlay that interprets signals from 80 different factors, including rates, currencies, stocks and commodities. Late September, that model too suggested a reduction in beta - stocks that exaggerate market moves in any direction - and to move up the quality spectrum.

Dale is concerned that markets are having to digest a slowdown in the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, specifically identifying data centers as well as the situation with Nvidia (NVDA) and issues surrounding its chip sales. Yet, he observes earnings forecasts for 2027 are still at or near the cycle highs.

At some point, when markets are convinced about the direction of rates, the markets may well rip, Dale says and when they do the things to buy will be semiconductors SOX, Korea KR:180721, Taiwan XX:180909, base metals , bitcoin and other crypto currencies. For now, though, "the signals are not telling us to put on risk."

-Jules Rimmer

data.title: The AI stock crash is mostly over, JPMorgan says - but a worse phase could be coming in 2027
data.description:
By Steve Goldstein

'Three phases of the bear' framework points to a rebound, but then a drift lower

JPMorgan's European quants expect a rebound followed by a drift lower.

The crash in artificial-intelligence stocks has just about run its course, but a worse phase could be in store for next year.

That's the conclusion of a team led by Khuram Chaudhry, head of European quantitative strategy at JPMorgan. Though the research was focused on European equities, it has obvious parallels with the action in the larger U.S. stock market.

They point to a "three phrases of the bear" framework, which are crash, rebound and drift lower. That was the case of the drawdowns during the dot-com bubble, the global financial crisis, the pandemic and then the 2022 rates shock/Russian invasion.

"Historically, this process lasts on average about 18 months, and we feel the recent momentum sell-off is likely a re-emergence of this first stage (crash), and a shift to the second stage (rebound) may soon follow," they say.

That looked to be the case on Friday, with U.S. stock-market futures (ES00) (NQ00) rallying and the Stoxx Europe 600 XX:SXXP up over 1%.

Looking at the current situation, the strategists say the bank's own measure of global investor sentiment has only been this depressed on five prior occasions in the last 20 years, each during a major growth shock.

They noted that fundamentals - either in the form of analyst earnings estimates or in the purchasing managers indexes - do not support such a downturn. That supports a rebound.

But this rebound may then be met with a drift lower. "We believe a regime change is underway, with an economic growth slowdown being the main risk to global markets in 2027, particularly if central banks run the risk of tightening into a slowing growth phase," they say.

During such a regime change, macro indicators will be volatile, and during peaks and troughs in the cycle data is notoriously mixed and fickle, they say.

They say JPMorgan's U.S. quant macro index is in expansion territory, but near levels where mean reversion is expected. The ratio of orders to inventories in the U.S. Institute for Supply Management manufacturing index has already peaked, even though the headline index remains healthy.

"For now, the fragility of growth is not a consensus view, with markets pricing in more than two rate hikes through the first quarter. In our view, tighter policy adds to the threat of a deeper slowdown, and may be a policy mistake. If activity slows more than expected, further downside - and a drift to new lows - cannot be ruled out," they say.

-Steve Goldstein

data.title: European Midday Briefing: Sentiment Calms, Stocks Rally as Volatile Week Winds Down
data.description:
MARKET WRAPS

European stocks were gaining Friday and were on track to extend gains achieved in the prior day's session, as sentiment appeared to stabilize.

Tech and industrial stocks were lifting European indexes higher heading into the end of what was a volatile week for the artificial intelligence trade.

Easing AI jitters helped lift miners in London. The calmer mood also revived risk appetite across cryptocurrencies and boosted Asian equities and precious metals.

Despite the technical signs of a possible recovery, XTB maintains that the fundamental problems surrounding the AI trade remain.

"The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered, for example, concerns about the profitability of the AI trade and financing costs."

Though the sustainability of spending on data centers and other AI-related infrastructure remains a key focus across markets, "data across the globe suggests that may not be an issue in the near term," ANZ said.

Approaching midday the FTSE 100, the CAC 40 and the DAX and the pan-European Stoxx 600 index were in positive territory.

Oil prices increased ahead of a meeting of OPEC and its allies this weekend. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Thursday an attack on the Jazan oil refinery sparked a fire and temporarily halted some operations.

Economic Insight

Inflation in France fell more than expected in November. Consumer prices in the eurozone's second-largest economy were 3.2% higher than in the same month of 2025.

The new European Central Bank president is likely to act more as a driving force, similar to Mario Draghi, rather than Christine Lagarde's consensus-oriented approach, Neuberger said.

"In practice, we believe this could make the ECB more responsive: it may tighten policy more quickly when inflation rises and ease policy more quickly when growth weakens."

It added that it also expected the ECB to raise interest rates in December but that there would be fewer rate hikes next year than are currently priced in.

U.S. Markets:

Stock futures gained across major U.S. indexes ahead of the opening bell for a shortened Black Friday session.

Forex:

The euro firmed slightly against the dollar, though with room to weaken on a six- to 12-month horizon, Danske Bank said, adding the most important upside risk to the euro against the greenback would be a sharp downturn in the U.S. economic growth outlook.

The dollar was little changed.

"While the initial U.S. dollar strength was driven by expectations of the Federal Reserve's tighter monetary policy stance, the move has cooled as markets have had time to digest what it might mean for growth down the line," Danske Bank said.

Bonds:

Treasury yields climbed on as markets reopened for a shortened session following the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eurozone government bond yields tracked their U.S. peers. Upward pressure on yields was also coming from higher oil prices.

The 10-year Treasury yield may have seen its cycle peak, SEB said.

"The bond rally since mid-November has been fueled by the equity sell-off, perceived risks of overtightening and lower inflation expectations.We are hesitant to bet on a sustained downtrend until closer to the policy rate peak."

The Federal Reserve rate-path outlook should provide a firmer anchor for five-year rates, Societe Generale said.

"A restrictive policy path is already largely reflected in market pricing, leaving less room for five-year rates to rise materially without a further hawkish repricing of the Fed outlook."

Yields on gilts, meanwhile, climbed due to inflation worries.

Energy:

Crude oil prices rose leading into Sunday's OPEC meeting. Both Brent and West Texas Intermediate benchmarks were on track for their first weekly gain this month.

Metals:

Gold, silver and platinum prices surged as investors returned to the artificial-intelligence trade and global stocks rebounded, boosting risk appetite and easing pressure on assets that had been sold to meet liquidity needs.

Copper

Copper prices rallied, climbing back above the $12,000-a-metric-ton mark as stronger global equities boosted risk appetite.

Market focus remains on Chinese demand and inventories, as well as any flow of copper stocks held in the U.S. back into the global market.

EMEA HEADLINES

No Homes to Rent, No Way to Evict: Inside Spain's Housing Crisis

MADRID-In the spring of 2024, Sonia Moreira told her tenant of over a decade that she planned to sell her property, a top-floor, redbrick apartment in a working-class area outside the Spanish capital.

The tenant, Helizabet Delgado, refused to leave and stopped paying rent. Unemployed and facing health issues, she has benefited from housing laws designed to protect vulnerable tenants from eviction.

As Another Wartime Winter Sets In, Kyiv Residents Weigh Finally Leaving

KYIV-The last threads of Tetiana Limarova's frictionless world withered away this month as she found herself living on four hours of power a day.

Blow-drying her hair has become a luxury. Her Wi-Fi cuts out during the long blackouts, and when her power banks die she has to trek to the nearest mall to recharge her devices. Her 10-year-old son's schoolbag now includes a reading lamp for when the blackouts hit his elementary school.

Iranian Drone Attack Kills Two Italians in Kuwait

DUBAI-An Iranian drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italians performing maintenance on antidrone equipment, authorities said, as Tehran continues its attacks to pressure U.S. allies in the region.

The attack Thursday comes as Iran has maintained a stream of strikes targeting some of its Gulf neighbors and ships trying to get oil and natural gas out through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military and President Trump have said the strait remains open for business while keeping their strangling naval blockade in place against Iran.

Marlboro Maker Altria Explores Deal for Rival Imperial Brands

Altria said it was considering a cash bid to buy smaller London-listed peer Imperial Brands, a move that would expand the Marlboro maker's footprint selling cigarettes around the world.

Altria, based in Richmond, Va., has a market value of close to $127 billion and offers a range of brands including Marlboro cigarettes in the U.S., Skoal smokeless tobacco and NJOY e-cigarettes.

GLOBAL NEWS

The AI Boom Looks Alive and Well in Asia

TOKYO-Panic and euphoria swept global stock markets as the Jensen Huang drama unfolded, showing just how angsty investors have become over the durability of the artificial-intelligence boom.

Dig into the economic data coming out of Asia, however, and for now at least the economic burst from the technology is still going strong, even as worries deepen about the risk of a pullback and how bad an AI slump could get.

A Game-Changing Move Just Gave America the Edge Over China in AI

SINGAPORE-While the world was transfixed by Jensen Huang's fall and return to Nvidia, the U.S. government quietly took the upper hand in the artificial-intelligence race against China.

It did so with an update to Washington's export rules, closing a loophole that let Chinese companies legally tap as much as a quarter of their computing power by remotely accessing Nvidia chips in other countries, most notably Malaysia.

China's Industrial Profit Surged Despite Headwinds

China's industrial profit surged in October despite mounting domestic headwinds, as robust global demand for its tech products continued to turbocharge exports.

Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 20.1% from a year earlier in October, accelerating from the prior month's 14.4% growth, according to official data released Friday. During the first 10 months of the year, China's industrial profit jumped 16.0%.

Pensions Trusted by Millions of Industrial Workers Make a Surprising Comeback

Five years ago, millions of truckers, miners and other American industrial workers were in such grave danger of having their pensions cut that Congress injected cash. The real rescue came from the U.S. stock market.

Years of double-digit market gains have spurred a remarkable turnaround for multiemployer retirement plans, those pensions governed by collective bargaining agreements between a group of employers and a union. These funds fell into a dangerous limbo after suffering severe losses in the 2008-09 financial crisis, and amid the decadeslong decline of industries like mining and manufacturing.

Pennsylvania Races to Stem Measles Outbreak as Amish Wedding Season Draws Crowds

BELLEVILLE, Pa.-As measles cut a path through unvaccinated swaths of Pennsylvania this summer, Jonas Kurtz made sure all seven of his children had received the two shots needed for immunity.

Since then, none has contracted the highly contagious disease. But several unvaccinated members of his extended family came down with the telltale rash and fever following a home wedding attended by hundreds. The host had apparently caught the virus at a horse auction in Lancaster County-the epicenter of the state's outbreak.

DUBAI-An Iranian drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italians performing maintenance on antidrone equipment, authorities said, as Tehran continues its attacks to pressure U.S. allies in the region.

The attack Thursday comes as Iran has maintained a stream of strikes targeting some of its Gulf neighbors and ships trying to get oil and natural gas out through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military and President Trump have said the strait remains open for business while keeping their strangling naval blockade in place against Iran.

data.title: Fifth Yan'an Forum on Rural Development Explores AI's Role in Agriculture and Rural Industries
data.description:
Fifth Yan'an Forum on Rural Development Explores AI's Role in Agriculture and Rural Industries

Fifth Yan'an Forum on Rural Development Explores AI's Role in Agriculture and Rural Industries

PR Newswire

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 27, 2026

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From growing apples to selling them through QR codes, digital technology is transforming Yan'an's apple industry. How AI might take that further was the central question at the Fifth Yan'an Forum on Rural Development, held on November 14 at Northwest University. The forum drew nearly 500 participants, including scholars, entrepreneurs, and a generation of rural practitioners known in China as "new farmers".

The Yan'an University Rural Development Institute, Peking University HSBC Business School (PHBS), and Northwest University's School of Economics and Management co-hosted the forum with support from the Xi'an Rural Development Charity Foundation.

Hai Wen, vice chairman of the Peking University Council, founding dean of PHBS, and dean of Yan'an University's Rural Development Institute, chaired the forum. Over five years, the forum has connected scholars, entrepreneurs, philanthropists, and rural practitioners around practical challenges, he noted.

Sun Qingwei, president of Northwest University, said the forum would help advance agricultural and rural modernization by sharing research findings and lessons from successful practices. Wang Yanfeng, vice president of Yan'an University, said technology research must move beyond academic papers to improve practices in fields, barns, and processing lines and help raise local incomes.

In the keynote session, Wang Zhongmin, former vice chairman of the National Council for Social Security Fund, discussed the digital transformation of Yan'an's apple industry, and said AI agents could cut production and transaction costs, improve digital agricultural data and credit systems, and help farmers reach global markets and financing. Fan Gang, professor of economics at Peking University, examined how urbanization, land and social security reform, and technology can mobilize rural resources, raise incomes, and narrow the urban-rural gap.

Wei Wei, professor of management and vice chairman of the PHBS Council, outlined four stages of AI transformation for agribusiness — upgrading, transforming, restructuring, and reinventing. The dividing line, he said, is whether data and processes close the loop, and whether farmers share the gains.

Two roundtables — "Technology for Good, Connecting the World" and "Technology Revitalizing Villages, Philanthropy Pooling Strength" — drew participants from business, academia, international organizations including UNDP China, and charitable organizations. They discussed market links and cross-sector partnerships.

Launched in 2019, the forum has moved from Yan'an to Shenzhen, Beijing, and Xi'an. PHBS will continue to support the institute and work with universities, businesses, and foundations on technology-enabled agriculture and rural revitalization.

The Long March, 90 Years On: An Epic Journey Driven by Ideals and Unwavering Faith

The Long March, 90 Years On: An Epic Journey Driven by Ideals and Unwavering Faith

PR Newswire

BEIJING, Nov. 27, 2026

BEIJING, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In 2026, China marks the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's victory in the Long March. Ninety years ago, the Red Army marched through much of China while engaging in numerous battles. Despite extraordinarily harsh conditions, the Red Army helped change the course of the country's history.
